Looking at this problem, I need to find at which depth levels breaking the seal is optimal.

**Setup.** Levels 1–5, with Level 6 = success, Level 0 = failure. Standard thruster: ±1 with probability 1/2 each. Sealed module contains Heavy-Drive (always deeper) or Light-Drive (always shallower), each with probability 1/2. Breaking the seal forces use of the experimental thruster for that minute; afterward either thruster may be chosen freely.

**Value of breaking the seal at level n.** If Heavy-Drive (prob 1/2): move to n+1, then use Heavy-Drive every minute → guaranteed success, value 1. If Light-Drive (prob 1/2): forced to move to n−1; Light-Drive is useless afterward (always shallower, never helps), so continue with standard-only, value (n−1)/6 (gambler's ruin), or 0 if n−1 = 0. Thus

$$B(n) = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot \max(n-1,0)/6 = \frac{n+5}{12}, \qquad B(1)=\tfrac12.$$

**Dynamic program.** Let V(n) be the optimal success probability starting at level n with the seal intact, V(0)=0, V(6)=1:

$$V(n) = \max\!\Big(B(n),\;\tfrac12 V(n-1)+\tfrac12 V(n+1)\Big).$$

This is an obstacle problem; its solution is the smallest superharmonic majorant of B on {1,…,5} with the boundary values.

**Solving.** I test the hypothesis that breaking is optimal only at n=1, with V(2),…,V(5) given by the harmonic (linear) interpolation between V(1)=1/2 and V(6)=1:
$$V(n)=\tfrac25+\tfrac{n}{10},\quad\text{i.e. } V(1)=\tfrac12,\; V(2)=\tfrac35,\; V(3)=\tfrac7{10},\; V(4)=\tfrac45,\; V(5)=\tfrac9{10}.$$

Verify each level (standard branch S(n)=½V(n−1)+½V(n+1)):

| n | B(n) | S(n) | max = V(n) | optimal |
|---|------|------|------------|---------|
| 1 | 1/2 = 0.500 | ½·0+½·(3/5) = 0.300 | 0.500 | **break** |
| 2 | 7/12 ≈ 0.583 | ½·(1/2)+½·(7/10) = 3/5 = 0.600 | 0.600 | standard |
| 3 | 2/3 ≈ 0.667 | ½·(3/5)+½·(4/5) = 7/10 = 0.700 | 0.700 | standard |
| 4 | 3/4 = 0.750 | ½·(7/10)+½·(9/10) = 4/5 = 0.800 | 0.800 | standard |
| 5 | 5/6 ≈ 0.833 | ½·(4/5)+½·1 = 9/10 = 0.900 | 0.900 | standard |

All five equations are satisfied, and at every level the max is strict (no ties). Since the obstacle problem has a unique solution, this is the answer.

**Why only n=1.** At low levels the gambler's-ruin baseline is small, so the 50% chance of a guaranteed success via Heavy-Drive dominates. At higher levels the baseline is already large, and—crucially—*not* breaking preserves the option to break later if the sub drifts back down to Level 1. Breaking early forfeits this option and risks the Light-Drive penalty (losing a level, or instant failure at n=1's neighbor). The option value makes the standard continuation strictly better for n = 2,3,4,5.

**Conclusion.** The set S of levels where breaking the seal is part of the optimal strategy is S = {1}, so

$$\sum_{n\in S} n = 1.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
